strengths: Identifies a clean and useful product-manifold structure underlying the Cholesky manifold (Euclidean strictly-lower-triangular part × n copies of R++), providing a principled and general design space for new SPD metrics rather than an ad hoc construction.

Proposes two new metrics (θ-PCM and (θ,M)-BWCM) with fully closed-form Riemannian operators (geodesics, log/exp maps, parallel transport, weighted Fréchet mean) and gyrovector operations, rigorously proven to satisfy gyrovector space axioms (Thms 3.7, 4.1).

Introduces a diagonal power deformation that smoothly interpolates between the new metrics and the well-established Log-Cholesky Metric, offering a principled and tunable trade-off with theoretical justification (Lem. 3.5).

Strong and broad empirical validation: SPD MLR classifiers and residual blocks on multiple backbones (SPDNet, GyroSPD, RResNet) across three datasets (Radar, HDM05, FPHA), consistently outperforming AIM/LEM/LCM baselines while matching or improving efficiency.

Thorough numerical stability analysis (synthetic geodesics with near-degenerate eigenvalues) convincingly demonstrates the practical benefit of replacing diagonal log/exp with diagonal power operations, with dramatic differences in failure rates.

Detailed complexity analysis (asymptotic + empirical wall-clock) substantiates efficiency claims, showing the new metrics scale better than eigen-based methods (AIM, BWM) and are competitive with or faster than LCM at scale.

Extensive ablations (θ sweep, M in BWCM, diagonal statistics analysis) and tensor interpolation experiments add depth and help explain when/why the deformation parameter matters, improving interpretability of the method.
Comprehensive and well-organized appendix with full proofs, reproducibility details, and dataset/implementation specifics supports rigor and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution—replacing diagonal logarithm/exponentiation with diagonal power operations—is conceptually incremental relative to existing LCM and PEM/GBWM constructions, even though the product-structure framing and full operator suite are valuable.

The optimal deformation factor θ varies substantially and non-intuitively across datasets and backbones (Table 7, e.g., -1.5 to 0.75), indicating a nontrivial hyperparameter search is needed in practice, which partially undercuts the simplicity/practicality narrative.

Accuracy gains over LCM are sometimes modest or mixed (e.g., FPHA with θ-BWCM on SPDNet is roughly on par with LCM; Radar with θ-BWCM underperforms LCM/AIM in some settings), suggesting the practical benefit is dataset- and metric-choice dependent.
The learnable M in BWCM (Table 14, Sec. E.6) shows negligible or inconsistent benefit over M=I, raising questions about the practical value of the generalized (θ,M)-BWCM beyond the simpler θ-PCM.
Residual block comparison (Table 4) reports only a single best-of-three result rather than mean±std as used elsewhere, making this comparison less statistically rigorous than the rest of the paper.

The numerical stability experiments rely on synthetic worst-case scenarios (artificially tiny eigenvalues); while illustrative, it is unclear how often such extreme conditions arise in the real training regimes actually used in the classification experiments, leaving the practical impact of this stability advantage somewhat unquantified in the main learning tasks.
